title: The Day After Announcing 20 Percent: “I Don’t Like Fees.” Even So, Crude Oil Stayed High
part1:
There were two days in the crude oil market that felt like a fast-press quiz. On July 13, a big number suddenly appeared. The next day, July 14, that number was replaced by a different card. But Brent crude futures did not smoothly return to their previous level.

First, July 13. Mr. Trump posted that the United States would seek a 20 percent reimbursement from all cargoes passing through the Strait of Hormuz, as payment for the cost of keeping the strait safe.

However, no one had yet been chosen to pay, and no way to collect the money had been decided. The details of the system, such as who would pay and how the amount would be calculated, were not given. What first jumped into the market was not an actual fee, but the striking number of 20 percent.
part2:
That day, Brent crude futures rose 9.59 percent and settled at $83.30 a barrel. Reuters linked the rise to the US sea blockade of Iran, which was expected to begin the next day, and to concerns about energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. We cannot say for sure that the 20 percent plan alone caused the rise.

Then, on the next day, July 14, the situation changed quickly. Mr. Trump announced that the reimbursement fee would be replaced with trade and investment deals between the Gulf states and the United States. He also said that no one should charge ships passing through the strait, and that he did not like the idea of fees itself. The plan announced the day before had been changed into another form the next day.
part3:
If crude oil had fallen sharply at this point, the story would have been simple. But after the announcement, Brent gave back only part of its gains. It soon returned to a high level close to where it had been before the announcement. At the time the article was published, it was up about 2.6 percent, at more than $85 a barrel. The settlement price on July 14 was also $84.73, up 1.7 percent from the day before.

The card showing the fee plan was taken off the table for a while. Even so, the sea blockade, attacks between the United States and Iran, tanker safety, and concerns about energy shipments through the strait continued that day. So although the market reacted to the withdrawal of the plan, the factors surrounding the strait had not disappeared.

News about a distant strait moved the figure for a global crude-oil benchmark. On top of that, the policy plan disappeared, but the price returned to a high level. What made this episode interesting was that the news and the market reaction seemed to be reading completely different scripts.
in_one_line: Although the proposed Strait of Hormuz fee was withdrawn, Brent crude remained high amid continuing regional tensions.
